extracted.intended_audience: Reformers, theologians, clergy, and informed lay Christians (participants in ecclesiastical councils and doctrinal debates).
extracted.subtask_description: A set of confessional/doctrinal articles laying out Lutheran positions on sin, law, repentance, sacraments, church offices, and related practices — intended as the authoritative stance to be defended before councils and adversaries. The page enumerates individual articles with scriptural citations, polemical critique of Papal/Scholastic positions, and practical prescriptions for church life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Sin originated from one man Adam; by his disobedience all men became sinners, subject to death and the devil (original or capital sin). The fruits of this sin are evil deeds forbidden in the Ten Commandments (unbelief, idolatry, lack of fear of God, presumption, despair, blindness, lying, false swearing, neglect of prayer and God's Word, disobedience to parents, murder, unchastity, theft, deception, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original sin is a deep corruption of nature that reason cannot understand and must be learned from Scripture (Ps. 51:5; Rom. 6; Gen. 3). Rejects scholastic/philosophical errors that claim: natural powers remain intact, man has right reason and good will by nature, free will can do good and refrain from evil, natural powers can keep God's commands, good intention is unnecessary for sacraments, or that the Holy Ghost is not necessary for good works. If those scholastic teachings were true, Christ's death would be in vain; hence they are condemned. (Explains why original sin necessitates Christ's work.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Of the Law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law was given by God to restrain sin by threats and promise of punishment and offer of grace/benefit, but sin renders this ineffective in many. The chief office of the Law is to reveal original sin and show man's utter corruption and inability to regard God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Law either restrains some by fear of punishment (those who would otherwise do worse) or exposes hypocrisy (those who think they can keep the Law by natural powers). The Law works wrath and increases sin when presented alone (Rom. 4:15; Rom. 5:20). Its purpose is to terrify and drive people to despair so they may seek aid in the Gospel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance is the Law's office retained by the New Testament: the Holy Spirit reproves the world of sin, bringing true sorrow and 'passiva contritio' (true inward anguish and humiliation). True repentance drives all people to see themselves as lost and to desire the remission of sins through the Gospel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True repentance is not manufactured (activa contritio) but a crushing of conscience and a conviction of total guilt. It must be accompanied by the consolatory promise of grace through the Gospel (Mark 1:15; Luke 24:47). Distinguishes true repentance from false/partial repentance; true repentance heaps 'all' sin together and cannot be uncertain or piecemeal. Repentance continues throughout life as believers contend with remaining sin by the gift of the Holy Ghost. Also warns against sectarian claims that faith permits deliberate sin or that a person who sins after believing necessarily never had true faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Repentance of the Papists
rubrics_metrics.description: The Papal system treats repentance as penance for actual sins only and defines three parts: contrition, confession, and satisfaction; it teaches that if one truly repents, confesses, and renders satisfaction one merits forgiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This system is criticized as teaching confidence in human works rather than Christ: contrition is often uncertain or replaced by 'attrition' (half-contrition), confession requires an impossible enumeration of all sins leading to lifelong uncertainty, and satisfaction is arbitrary and insufficient (leading to reliance on purgatory). Indulgences and the sale of remission (golden jubilee) are condemned as commercializing salvation and creating false confidence. Anti-patterns: treating attrition as full contrition, relying on enumeration and works for absolution, trusting indulgences and purchased satisfactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of the Gospel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gospel aids against sin in multiple ways: first, by the spoken Word which proclaims forgiveness; second, through Baptism; third, through the Sacrament of the Altar; fourth, through the power of the keys; and also through mutual conversation and consolation of brethren.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the primacy of the spoken Word and Gospel promise in bringing consolation and remission of sins (contrasts with Law alone which brings despair). The Gospel operates through Word and Sacraments to deliver redemption (Ps. 130).

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Baptism
rubrics_metrics.description: Baptism is the Word of God in the water, a washing in the Word commanded by Christ. Children ought to be baptized because they belong to the promised redemption through Christ and the Church should administer it to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects views that attribute intrinsic spiritual power to water apart from the Word (rejects some Dominican and Franciscan teachings and Scotist positions). Emphasizes that Baptism's efficacy is the Word's working in the element, not an independent natural power of the water or divine will apart from Word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of the Sacrament of the Altar
rubrics_metrics.description: Bread and wine in the Lord's Supper are the true body and blood of Christ and are given and received by both godly and wicked Christians. Both forms (bread and wine) should be given; one form alone is not the whole ordinance instituted by Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the scholastic subtlety of transubstantiation that bread and wine lose their natural substance and only appearances remain. Affirms that Scripture speaks of 'the bread which we break' (1 Cor. 10:16) and that the presence of bread remains. Condemns those who omit or prohibit either form and who elevate such innovation above Scripture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of the Keys
rubrics_metrics.description: The keys are an office and power given by Christ to the Church for binding and loosing sins, including subtle and hidden sins known only to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only God can rightly judge the extent and weight of sins; human judgment is limited (Ps. 143:2; 1 Cor. 4:4). The office of the keys is therefore an ordained church power but must be exercised with humility recognizing God's prerogative in judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Confession and the Absolution (power of the keys) are aids ordained by Christ and should not be abolished; they are particularly helpful for tender consciences and the untrained young for examination and instruction in Christian doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The enumeration of sins should be left free to the individual (one may confess more or less as one wishes). Private absolution should be esteemed. Emphasizes that God grants His Spirit or grace only through or with the preceding outward Word (to guard against enthusiasts who claim Spirit before Word). Warns against enthusiasts who claim direct Spirit apart from preaching and Scripture and against Papal claims of inward authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Excommunication
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater excommunication (as the Pope calls it) is regarded only as a civil penalty; the true Christian excommunication excludes manifest and obstinate sinners from the Sacrament and other communion of the Church until they amend their lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers should not mix secular punishments with ecclesiastical excommunication. Excommunication's ecclesiastical form is remedial/pastoral (to prompt amendment), not a vehicle for secular or political coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Ordination and the Call
rubrics_metrics.description: If bishops rightly discharged their office, it might be fitting for them to ordain and confirm preachers for love and unity, but not necessarily. Because many bishops are worldly and neglect spiritual duties, the Church ought not to remain without ministers and may ordain suitable persons itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically the Church has examples (e.g., Alexandria) where priests and preachers governed without bishops; even laws say ordinations by heretics remain valid. The practical guidance is that lack of episcopal cooperation does not invalidate the Church's need and right to provide ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of the Marriage of Priests
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition of marriage (perpetual celibacy) for clergy lacks authority and is tyrannical; it has produced innumerable sins of unchastity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that forbidding marriage is beyond human authority and has caused widespread abuse; therefore marriage should be free as instituted by God. Cites 1 Tim. 4 to label the prohibition a 'doctrine of devils.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Of the Church
rubrics_metrics.description: Denies that the Papacy constitutes the Church; the Church is the assembly of holy believers (the lambs who hear the Shepherd). Holiness consists in the Word of God and true faith, not in albs, tonsures, long gowns, or ceremonial inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects Papal claims to define Church membership by ceremonies and external marks. Emphasizes that a seven-year-old child can know the Church: it is believers hearing Christ the Shepherd; liturgical or clerical trappings do not define holiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: How One is Justified before God, and of Good Works
rubrics_metrics.description: One is justified before God by faith: by faith we acquire a new and clean heart and God accounts us righteous and holy for the sake of Christ our Mediator. Though sin in the flesh remains, God does not remember or punish it for Christ's sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good works naturally follow true faith; if good works do not follow, faith is false. Any sinful or imperfectness in works is not reckoned by God for Christ's sake. Boasting in merits apart from grace is condemned (1 Cor. 1:31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Monastic Vows
rubrics_metrics.description: Monastic vows conflict with the chief article (justification by faith) and therefore must be abolished. A vow to live holier than ordinary Christians seeks to earn heaven by works and thus denies Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condemns teachings (e.g., St. Thomas' claim) that a monastic vow is equal to Baptism as blasphemy. Monastic vows promote a false righteousness and are to be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Human Traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Human traditions that are said to serve for the remission of sins or to merit salvation are unchristian and condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Christ's condemnation of teachings that substitute human commandments for God's Word (Matt. 15:9) and Titus 1:14. Declaring breaking such ordinances a mortal sin is wrong. Human traditions should not be treated as salvific requirements.
